cards.name: Psoriasis
short: T cells release IL-23, IL-17 and TNF-α, so keratinocytes divide too fast.
Sharp-edged red plaques with silvery scale on elbows and knees.
Severity is graded by BSA: 5%, 8% and 10% are the cut-offs.
Order of treatment: topicals, then an oral systemic agent, then a biologic, then PUVA.
Before any biologic: TB screening, and no live vaccines.

steps.title: Who gets it, and what sets it off
steps.q: Which drugs can bring psoriasis on, what is the Koebner response, and which comorbidities come with it?
steps.src: Smith Pathophys slides 20, 24, 26; Patel Scaly slides 21, 24–25; 11/11 lecture

rows: Alcohol, smoking, obesity or metabolic syndrome
Injury to the skin (her example: a horsefly bite)
Drugs that can bring it on
[[psa|Psoriatic arthritis]]: “a common condition that may occur over time”
Inflammatory bowel diseases: Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis
About {{30%}} have a first-degree relative with psoriasis
Lesions begin at previously clear sites after trauma: friction, venipuncture, bites, surgery, pressure
Asymmetric: hands, feet, knees; no rheumatoid factor elevation

steps.title: What goes wrong
steps.q: Which cytokines drive it, and how fast do the keratinocytes turn over?
steps.src: Smith Pathophys slides 19, 21–23; Smith PCol slides 66–74

rows: Keratinocytes multiply too fast and do not finish differentiating
Psoriasis: divide in {{1.5 days}}, shed in {{4 days}}

blocks.label: Watch how it works: where each cytokine biologic binds

items: Dr. Patel: psoriasis has the fastest epidermal turnover of the three scaly conditions (11/10 and 11/11 lectures).

steps.title: How it looks, and how she grades it
steps.q: What are the three BSA cut-offs, and where do 7% and 9% fall?

rows: Red-violet, symmetrical, {{sharp borders}} (well demarcated), at least 0.5 cm across
Single lesions at the {{knees and elbows}}, or generalized; also scalp, trunk, lower extremities
In more than 50% of patients; can be severe
★ “it has been corrected to 10% … I want you to follow this slide”
The provider takes the plaque-covered area as a share of the whole body
PASI and DLQI also mark severe at 10: “I only want you to know the BSA”

steps.title: Treat it: her order of treatment
steps.q: Name the four lines in order, say where each algorithm starts, and say what moves a patient to the next line.

rows: Lower stress; regular exercise; weight management (BMI 18.5–24.9)
Moisturizers; oatmeal baths; sunscreen SPF 30+ with UVA protection
Age, severity, location of lesions, comorbidities, past and current treatment, cost
Systemic agent is the last line, with the topical continued
Slide 35 also shows topical agents + phototherapy as the middle step (not spoken in class)
Moderate after the topical agents have been tried, or severe
Starts with a systemic agent (“most likely methotrexate”) ± a topical agent
Then a more potent systemic agent or a biologic
Biologic considered earlier with comorbidities such as psoriatic arthritis
Moisturizers; continue if controlled; step down to the lowest dose or potency that keeps control

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: Topical agents (mild to moderate)
pts: ★ Corticosteroids are the {{most effective}}
Low potency on the face and skin folds
Limit to {{≤ 4 weeks}} and limit the surface area
The choice depends on what was tried before and what is used now
facts: How each is applied
Corticosteroid: 2–4 times daily; cream or lotion by day, ointment at night
Calcipotriene: ointment once or twice daily; cream or foam twice daily
Tazarotene (or adapalene): once daily at bedtime
Anthralin: thick plaques only, 2 hours or less, then wiped off; zinc oxide around the edges
Coal tar: on in the evening, washed off in the morning
Salicylic acid: shampoo for scalp lesions
Pimecrolimus: intertriginous areas
pick: Anthralin: on for 2 hours or less, then wiped off; zinc oxide around the edges
Steroid stepped up in potency for about a month, little change
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: the psoriasis is moderate and the topical agents have been tried, or it is severe. Topical steroids are limited to 4 weeks, and she contacts the patient at 1–2 weeks.

blocks.label: Next
blocks.title: Oral systemic agent, with the topical continued
pts: ★ {{Methotrexate}} is usually first (most affordable)
Give {{folic acid}} 1–5 mg daily with it
“That topical medication’s always going to be continued”
No fixed order among the systemic agents: chosen by age and safety profile
Abatacept, on the same slides, is a subcutaneous injection: TB screening; interacts with live vaccines
pick: Untreated hypertension, systemic malignancy or infection
Not acitretin: no pregnancy within {{3 years}} after stopping
Tofacitinib (JAK inhibitor); not with a biologic; no live vaccines
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: topicals and an oral systemic agent have failed.

blocks.label: Then
blocks.title: Biologic
pts: ★ “Know the generic name, know the brand name, and know what class they fall in”
blocks.warn: ★ TNF-α inhibitors: contraindicated in congestive heart failure (“I’m saying this twice for a reason”).
facts: Before the first dose
Screen for {{TB}}; [[ppd|PPD]] repeated every year
No {{live vaccines}} (vaccines that are not live are allowed)
TNF-α inhibitors: hepatitis B screening
While on it
Stop during an active infection (flu, cold, COVID)
Monitor CBC and LFTs
Common: injection site reaction, headache, rhinitis, upper respiratory infection
pick: No TNF-α inhibitor (adalimumab and its class)
Demyelinating disease or MS, in the patient or a first-degree relative
{{Brodalumab}} carries a boxed warning for suicide risk and needs a [[rems|REMS]]
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: the psoriasis is severe and [[refractory|refractory]].

blocks.label: Last
blocks.title: [[puva|PUVA]]
pts: Oral psoralen plus UVA
“Absolute last line”: severe, refractory psoriasis
About {{90%}} respond
Skin biopsy first, to confirm psoriasis
Risk: serious burns, blistering, peeling

blocks.text: After starting any treatment: contact the patient in 1–2 weeks.

patients.t: A 52-year-old woman has two new 2 cm plaques with silvery scale, one on each elbow. BSA is 7%. No treatment has been tried this time.
patients.w: 7% is mild to moderate and nothing has been tried, so treatment starts with a topical agent. Her poll answer for this patient was a topical corticosteroid.

x.A biologic: A biologic comes after topical and oral systemic agents have failed.
x.PUVA: PUVA is the absolute last line, for severe psoriasis that nothing else has controlled.
x.An oral systemic agent: An oral systemic agent comes after the topical agents have been tried in moderate psoriasis, or in severe psoriasis.

patients.t: A 34-year-old man has plaques with silvery scale on the trunk and legs. The provider calculates a BSA of 9%.
patients.w: Moderate starts at 8% and severe at 10%. “Like a 9%, right? So in between that moderate as well as severe.”

x.Mild: Mild is a BSA of 5% or less.
x.Mild to moderate: Mild to moderate is a BSA between 5% and 8%, such as her 7% poll patient.
x.Severe: Severe is a BSA of 10% or more.

patients.t: A patient has moderate psoriasis. Topical corticosteroids, calcipotriene and coal tar have been used, and the plaques remain.
patients.w: Moderate psoriasis after the topical agents have been tried moves to an oral systemic agent, with the topical continued. Methotrexate is usually first.

x.A topical agent: The topical agents have already been tried; a topical is continued, with an oral agent added.
x.A biologic: A biologic comes after topical and oral systemic agents have failed.
x.PUVA: PUVA is the absolute last line, for severe psoriasis that nothing else has controlled.

patients.t: A patient has used topical agents and methotrexate. Neither has controlled the psoriasis.
patients.w: A biologic comes after topical and oral systemic agents have failed. Screen for TB before the first dose; no live vaccines.

x.A topical agent: Topical agents have already been tried and are not enough alone.
x.PUVA: PUVA is the absolute last line, for severe psoriasis that nothing else has controlled.
x.An oral systemic agent: An oral systemic agent (methotrexate) has already failed.

patients.t: A patient is about to start a biologic. The medical history includes congestive heart failure.
patients.w: Adalimumab is a TNF-α inhibitor, and TNF-α inhibitors are contraindicated in congestive heart failure (“I’m saying this twice for a reason”).

x.Ustekinumab (Stelara): Ustekinumab blocks IL-12 and IL-23; the heart failure warning is on the TNF-α inhibitors.
x.Secukinumab (Cosentyx): Secukinumab blocks IL-17A; its caution is Crohn’s disease.
x.Risankizumab (Skyriza): Risankizumab blocks IL-23; the heart failure warning is on the TNF-α inhibitors.

patients.t: A patient has severe psoriasis. Topical agents, an oral systemic agent and a biologic have all failed.
patients.w: PUVA (oral psoralen plus UVA) is the absolute last line, for severe refractory psoriasis.

x.An oral systemic agent: An oral systemic agent has already failed.

numbers: severe psoriasis (BSA); she first said 20%, then corrected it
anthralin stays on thick plaques, then is wiped off
apremilast response; titrated to 30 mg twice daily over the first week
no pregnancy after stopping acitretin; maximum response 3–6 months
contact the patient after starting treatment

cards.name: Dandruff
short: Malassezia fungi on the scalp; non-inflammatory; starts at puberty.
Thin white or grey flakes on the scalp only.
Mild (intermittent): non-medicated shampoo daily or every other day.
Moderate to severe (daily): medicated shampoo, left on 3–5 minutes.
Daily for 1 week, then 2–3 times weekly for 2–3 weeks, then once weekly.

steps.title: Cause and who
steps.q: Which organism is linked to dandruff, when does it start, and why can a non-inflammatory scalp look inflamed?

rows: Faster epidermal cell turnover and abnormal keratinization: flaking and [[pruritus|pruritus]]
Dry climate, cold temperature, stress; otherwise generally stable
{{Secondary}}, from scratching: “it’s not gonna be from the start of that condition”

items: ★ Dandruff has the slowest [[kinetics|epidermal turnover]] of the three scaly conditions; psoriasis the fastest. She asks the order only.

steps.title: Recognise it, and grade it
steps.q: What separates mild dandruff from moderate to severe dandruff?

rows: ★ Her poll: “Intermittent white flakes, right? Not daily”
Two groups only: “it’s either mild or it’s moderate to severe”

steps.title: Self-care, or something else?
steps.q: Which findings mean the flaking is not dandruff?

rows: Both grades are treated with a nonprescription shampoo
{{Yellow, oily}} scales on red skin, or scale beyond the scalp (face, trunk) → seborrheic dermatitis
{{Silvery-white}} scale on sharp-bordered red plaques → psoriasis
Scalp scaling in an infant → cradle cap; dandruff starts at {{puberty}}
Slide 51: a week after self-treatment begins; she said 1 to 2 weeks (11/11)

items: Her slides give a time to refer (worse, or longer than 7 days) on the seborrheic dermatitis slide, not on the dandruff slide.

steps.title: Treat it: match the shampoo to the severity
steps.q: What does each grade get, how long does a medicated shampoo stay on, and what is the weekly taper?
steps.src: Patel Scaly slides 7, 9; 11/10 lecture; Smith PCol slides 53, 57

rows: Slow the epidermal turnover of the scalp

blocks.label: Mild
blocks.title: Non-medicated shampoo
pts: ★ Her poll answer for intermittent flakes with no inflammation
{{Daily or every other day}}

blocks.label: Moderate to severe
blocks.title: OTC medicated shampoo
pts: Pyrithione zinc is the main ingredient in most OTC products
“There are many options available”: any of the three
facts: How to use it
Leave on the scalp {{3 to 5 minutes}}
Rinse well with water
Daily for {{1 week}}
Then {{2–3 times weekly}} for {{2 to 3 weeks}}
Then {{once weekly}} for control

blocks.label: Not effective
blocks.title: Hydrocortisone 1%
pts: ★ The dandruff “no” on her OTC chart: “Hydrocortisone 1%, not effective in dandruff”

patients.t: A young man sees white flakes on his dark clothing now and then. His scalp is not itchy and does not look inflamed. He takes no medications.
o: Baby oil massage and a soft brush
patients.w: Intermittent flakes with no inflammation is mild dandruff; mild dandruff gets a non-medicated shampoo daily or every other day (her poll).

x.A pyrithione zinc shampoo: A medicated shampoo is for moderate to severe dandruff: daily flakes with moderate–severe inflammation.
x.Baby oil massage and a soft brush: Oil massage and a soft bristle brush are the care for cradle cap in an infant.
x.Hydrocortisone 1% lotion: Hydrocortisone 1% is not effective for dandruff.

patients.t: A 30-year-old man has flakes every day, and his scalp is itchy and moderately inflamed. There are no yellow scales, and the skin off the scalp is clear.
o: Baby oil massage and a soft brush
patients.w: Daily dandruff with moderate–severe inflammation is moderate to severe; it gets an OTC medicated shampoo (pyrithione zinc, selenium sulfide or coal tar).

x.A non-medicated shampoo: A non-medicated shampoo is for mild, intermittent dandruff.
x.Baby oil massage and a soft brush: Oil massage and a soft bristle brush are the care for cradle cap in an infant.
x.Hydrocortisone 1% lotion: Hydrocortisone 1% is not effective for dandruff.

patients.t: The same man has used a selenium sulfide shampoo every day for 1 week and is improving.
patients.q: How should he use it now?
o: Stop, and restart if the flakes return
2–3 times weekly for 2–3 weeks, then once weekly
2–3 times weekly for 4 weeks, then once weekly
Daily for 3 more weeks, then stop
patients.w: Dandruff schedule: daily for 1 week, then 2–3 times weekly for 2 to 3 weeks, then once weekly for control.

x.Stop, and restart if the flakes return: The schedule tapers to once weekly for control; it does not stop after week 1.
x.2–3 times weekly for 4 weeks, then once: Four weeks at 2–3 times weekly is the seborrheic dermatitis schedule.
x.Daily for 3 more weeks, then stop: Daily use is for the first week only.

patients.t: A woman starting a pyrithione zinc shampoo for daily dandruff asks how long to leave it on her scalp.
o: Overnight, then rinse in the morning
patients.w: A medicated shampoo stays on the scalp 3 to 5 minutes and is then rinsed well with water.

x.Rinse it off at once: It must stay on 3 to 5 minutes before it is rinsed.
x.Overnight, then rinse in the morning: Evening on, morning off is coal tar for psoriasis plaques, not a dandruff shampoo.

patients.t: A patient with daily dandruff asks which of four OTC products on the shelf will not work for it.
patients.q: Which one is not effective for dandruff?
patients.w: Her OTC chart has two “no” cells: hydrocortisone 1% for dandruff, and sulfur for psoriasis.

x.Coal tar: Coal tar 0.5–5% is on the chart for dandruff.
x.Selenium sulfide: Selenium sulfide 1% is on the chart for dandruff.
x.Sulfur: Sulfur 2–5% is on the chart for dandruff; its “no” is psoriasis.

numbers: medicated shampoo stays on the scalp
daily use of the medicated shampoo
second stage of the dandruff taper
pyrithione zinc, rinse-off, for dandruff (0.1–0.25% residual)

cards.name: Seborrheic dermatitis (adolescents and adults)
short: Chronic inflammation where sebaceous glands are active; Malassezia.
Yellow, greasy scales on red skin: scalp, face, ears, chest.
Refer if it worsens or lasts longer than 7 days.
Scalp: ketoconazole shampoo first line. Face and body: antifungal cream.
Resistant: ketoconazole shampoo plus a corticosteroid lotion.

steps.title: Cause, who and triggers
steps.q: Who gets it, and which six risk factors or triggers are on her slide?

rows: Chronic {{inflammatory}} disorder in areas of sebaceous gland activity
{{Malassezia}}, a yeast-like fungus that grows in the sebum
Chronic, no specific cure; neither harmful nor contagious
Infants: see the cradle cap card
Change of season: worse in {{cold}} weather

items: ★ Second-fastest epidermal turnover of the three scaly conditions; she asks the order only.

steps.title: Recognise it
steps.q: What do the scales look like, and where are they?

rows: ★ {{Yellow, greasy}} scales in patches or plaques, with exudate and crusting
Head, ears and face, often with itching and stinging
Scalp, eyebrows, ear canal; yellowish scales in the nasolabial creases

items: ★ Her key words for the poll: “greasy, scaling, yellowish scales … as well as the location”.

steps.title: Self-care, or refer?
steps.q: After how many days without improvement is the patient referred?

rows: An adult starts with an {{OTC antifungal shampoo}}
★ “Again, the 7-day period comes into play, referral straight to healthcare provider”
OTC dandruff shampoos gave only temporary relief: she still chose the first-line shampoo, not referral

steps.title: Treat it: match the product to the site and the problem
steps.q: What is first line for the adult scalp, what is second line, and what is the schedule?

rows: Minimize or remove visible [[erythema|erythema]] and scaling

blocks.label: Thick scale or crust
blocks.title: Soften, then wash
pts: Soften with mineral oil or olive oil
Or a cream containing salicylic acid or sulfur
Wash the skin often: slide 15 says more often than twice daily; she said twice a day
Dishwashing liquid may be used on tough scale

blocks.label: Scalp
blocks.title: OTC antifungal shampoo
pts: ★ First line: {{ketoconazole}} shampoo (“first line is your key term here”)
Second line: selenium sulfide, pyrithione zinc, ciclopirox, coal tar
facts: How to use it
Leave on hair, scalp and affected areas {{3 to 5 minutes}}, then rinse; may repeat
Daily for {{1–2 weeks}}
Then 2–3 times a week for {{4 weeks}}
Improved after 4 weeks: {{once weekly}}
Not improved at 4 weeks: keep the same frequency

blocks.label: Face and body
blocks.title: Antifungal cream
pts: Topical {{antifungal creams}} to decrease fungal growth
Ultraviolet light therapy is also listed

blocks.label: Redness and itching
blocks.title: Topical corticosteroid
pts: Scalp: corticosteroid {{lotion}}
Other parts of the body: corticosteroid cream
Mild to potent
OTC chart: hydrocortisone 0.5–1%

blocks.label: Resistant
blocks.title: Combine the two
pts: Ketoconazole shampoo and a {{corticosteroid lotion}} must often be combined in therapy-resistant cases

patients.t: A 35-year-old man has itching, redness and scaling of the scalp, eyebrows and ear canal. OTC dandruff shampoos gave only temporary relief. There is greasy scale on the scalp and yellowish scale in the nasolabial creases.
patients.w: This is seborrheic dermatitis in an adult, and ketoconazole shampoo is first line (her poll: “first line is your key term here”).

x.Selenium sulfide shampoo: Selenium sulfide is second line for seborrheic dermatitis.
x.Pyrithione zinc shampoo: Pyrithione zinc is second line for seborrheic dermatitis.
x.Coal tar shampoo: Coal tar is second line for seborrheic dermatitis.

patients.t: A 40-year-old woman used ketoconazole shampoo daily for 2 weeks, then 2–3 times a week for 4 weeks. Her scalp is much improved.
patients.w: If there is improvement after 4 weeks, the frequency may be reduced to once weekly.

x.Stop the shampoo: The condition is chronic with no specific cure; the schedule steps down to once weekly.
x.Return to daily use: Daily use is the first 1–2 weeks.
x.Add a corticosteroid lotion: The lotion is added in therapy-resistant cases; she has improved.

patients.t: A 38-year-old man has yellow, greasy scales on red skin in the eyebrows and nasolabial folds. His scalp is clear.
patients.w: Face and body: topical treatment with antifungal creams. The shampoos are for the scalp.

x.A ketoconazole shampoo: Ketoconazole shampoo is first line for the scalp; his scalp is clear.
x.A coal tar shampoo: Coal tar shampoo is a second-line scalp product.
x.A non-medicated shampoo: A non-medicated shampoo is for mild dandruff and for infants.

patients.t: An adult’s scalp seborrheic dermatitis has not responded to ketoconazole shampoo alone, used as directed.
patients.w: Ketoconazole shampoo and a corticosteroid lotion must often be combined in therapy-resistant cases; lotion is the form for the scalp.

x.A corticosteroid cream: Corticosteroid creams are for other parts of the body; the scalp gets a lotion.
x.A sulfur cream: A sulfur cream softens scales; it is not the add-on for resistant cases.
x.Mineral oil: Mineral oil softens scales before washing.

patients.t: A 29-year-old man began ketoconazole shampoo 8 days ago for seborrheic dermatitis. The redness and scaling are worse.
patients.w: If the disorder worsens or symptoms persist longer than 7 days, a health care provider should be consulted.

x.Continue daily for 2 more weeks: He is worse and past 7 days, which is her point of referral.
x.Reduce to once weekly: Once weekly is for a patient who has improved after 4 weeks.
x.Switch to selenium sulfide: A second-line shampoo does not replace referral once the disorder has worsened.

numbers: shampoo stays on hair, scalp and affected areas
worse, or symptoms longer than this: see a health care provider
of adolescents and adults; men more than women
sulfur (dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis; not psoriasis)

cards.name: Cradle cap (seborrheic dermatitis in infants)
short: Seborrheic dermatitis of an infant’s scalp; neither harmful nor contagious.
Greasy or dry scaling, on the scalp only.
Daily: oil massage, non-medicated shampoo, soft bristle brush.
No corticosteroids and no ketoconazole in infants.
Severe cases only: salicylic acid 3–5% in olive oil or a water-soluble base.

steps.title: Cause and timing
steps.q: How long can it persist, and is it harmful or contagious?

rows: {{Seborrheic dermatitis}} in an infant: “think of the [[cradle-cap|cradle cap]]”
May persist up to {{30 months}} of age

steps.title: Recognise it
steps.q: How does cradle cap differ from seborrheic dermatitis in an adult?

rows: ★ The {{scalp}}: “infants, it’s only on the scalp”
{{Yellow}}, greasy scales on red skin of the head, ears, face and trunk
An infant a couple of weeks old with a scaly scalp: “this is an example of cradle cap”

steps.title: Treat it: daily care of the scalp and face
steps.q: List the three daily care steps for the scalp, and the care for the face.

blocks.label: Scalp, every day
blocks.title: Remove the scale
pts: ★ Massage the scalp with {{baby oil or vegetable oil}} (her poll answer)
Then shampoo with a {{non-medicated}} shampoo
Use a {{soft bristle brush}}
Mineral oil or olive oil also softens the scales

blocks.label: Face
blocks.title: Cleanser and emollient
pts: Wash with a {{mild soap or cleanser}}
Apply a facial [[emollient|emollient]]

items: “With our infants, we’re mostly using non-pharm therapy.”

steps.title: What is not used in infants, and severe cases
steps.q: Which two products are not used in infants, and what is the option for severe cases?

blocks.label: Not used
blocks.title: Corticosteroids and ketoconazole
pts: ★ Slide 18: “DO NOT suggest {{corticosteroids}}”; “Hydrocortisone, absolutely not”
★ “{{Ketoconazole}} shampoo is not recommended in infants”: it irritates infant skin
Face too: “We’re still not recommending corticosteroids cause remember the age parameter”
Nystatin ointment: “would not be beneficial”

blocks.label: Severe
blocks.title: Salicylic acid 3–5%
pts: {{Salicylic acid 3–5%}} in {{olive oil}} or a water-soluble base
“Severe cases only”: “an option if nothing else has worked”
Why last: an infant’s skin is thin, absorbs more, and is more prone to irritation

patients.t: A new mother brings an infant a couple of weeks old. The scalp has greasy scale, and the skin elsewhere is clear. She asks what to use on the scalp.
o: Baby oil massage, then non-medicated shampoo
patients.w: Infant care is non-drug: massage the scalp with baby oil or vegetable oil, then a non-medicated shampoo and a soft bristle brush (her poll).

x.Ketoconazole 1% shampoo, left on 3–5 min: “Ketoconazole shampoo is not recommended in infants.”
x.Hydrocortisone 1% cream, twice daily: Her slide: do not suggest corticosteroids. “Hydrocortisone, absolutely not.”
x.Selenium sulfide shampoo, twice weekly: Medicated shampoos are adult products; infants get a non-medicated shampoo.

patients.t: A 6-month-old’s thick cradle cap has not cleared after weeks of daily oil massage, non-medicated shampoo and a soft brush.
patients.q: Which option is there for a severe case?
patients.w: For severe cases only: salicylic acid 3–5% in olive oil or a water-soluble base.

x.Ketoconazole 1% shampoo daily: Ketoconazole is not recommended in infants.
x.Hydrocortisone 1% lotion daily: Corticosteroids are not suggested for infants.
x.Coal tar 0.5–5% shampoo daily: Coal tar is not on her infant slide; it is a medicated shampoo for adults.

patients.t: A 3-week-old has cradle cap and some scaling on the cheeks. The mother asks whether her own hydrocortisone 1% cream can go on the baby’s face.
patients.q: What do you recommend for the face?
o: Ketoconazole shampoo as a face wash
Mild cleanser, then a facial emollient
patients.w: On the face: wash with a mild soap or cleanser and apply a facial emollient. “We’re still not recommending corticosteroids cause remember the age parameter.”

x.Hydrocortisone 1% cream for 7 days: Corticosteroids are not suggested for infants, on the scalp or the face.
x.An antifungal cream twice daily: Antifungal creams for the face and body are for adults.
x.Ketoconazole shampoo as a face wash: Ketoconazole is not recommended in infants.

patients.t: The mother of a 2-month-old with cradle cap asks whether it is dangerous and whether her older child can catch it.
o: Not contagious, but needs a physician
patients.w: Seborrheic dermatitis is neither harmful nor contagious. In infants it may persist up to 30 months of age.

x.Not contagious, but needs a physician: It is not harmful; daily non-drug care is the treatment.
x.Contagious, and needs a physician: It is neither harmful nor contagious.

numbers: age up to which it may persist
salicylic acid in olive oil or a water-soluble base, severe cases only
oil massage, non-medicated shampoo, soft bristle brush
where cradle cap is; the adult form is on the head, ears, face and trunk

steroid.name: Topical corticosteroids

sm.text: Target: the glucocorticoid receptor. The drug–receptor complex binds the GRE, or keeps NF-κB and AP-1 off the DNA. Face: low potency (hydrocortisone 1%); body: medium potency (betamethasone valerate 0.1%).

sk.text: Steroid skeleton (rings A–C six-membered, D five-membered). Potency rises with a C1–C2 double bond, a 6α-halogen, a 9α-halogen and the 11β-OH.

pa.role: First line for mild to moderate psoriasis; the most effective topical; her poll answer for the 7% patient
pa.how: 2–4 times daily: cream or lotion by day, ointment at night. Low potency on the face and skin folds. Limit to ≤ 4 weeks and limit the surface area.

pa.role: Adults: reduces erythema and itching; combined with ketoconazole shampoo in therapy-resistant cases
pa.how: Lotion for the scalp; cream for other parts of the body; mild to potent.

counsel: Psoriasis: apply 2 to 4 times a day; a cream or lotion in the daytime and an ointment at night.
Psoriasis: low potency on the face and in skin folds.
Psoriasis: not longer than 4 weeks; limit the surface area treated.
Psoriasis: if about a month with stepped-up potency has changed little, another topical option is tried.
Psoriasis: follow-up contact in 1–2 weeks.
Seborrheic dermatitis: a lotion goes on the scalp, a cream on the body; moisturize after washing.
avoid: Infants with cradle cap: “DO NOT suggest corticosteroids” (slide 18)
Not for longer than 4 weeks in psoriasis (slide 36)
Withdrawal of corticosteroids can precipitate psoriasis (slide 24)

hydrocortisone.name: Hydrocortisone 0.5–1% (OTC)

sm.text: Target: the glucocorticoid receptor; the low-potency steroid, the one for the face (hydrocortisone 1%).

sk.text: Natural cortisol, the parent structure. Less than 15% is absorbed through skin. 11β-HSD converts it to inactive cortisone.

pa.role: Not effective: the dandruff “no” on her OTC chart
pa.how: Not used.

pa.role: OTC option, 0.5–1%, for redness and itching in adults
pa.how: Lotion for the scalp; cream for other parts of the body.

bsa: The share of the skin that is affected, as a percentage. Dr. Patel: “I only want you to know the BSA.”

puva: Oral psoralen followed by UVA light. The psoralen cross-links DNA under UVA.
plaque: A raised lesion. In plaque psoriasis: red-violet, at least 0.5 cm across, well demarcated, covered by silver flaking scale.
psa: Arthritis that develops over time in a patient with psoriasis. Dr. Smith: asymmetric, in the hands, feet and knees, without rheumatoid factor.

dmard: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug. Her slide labels methotrexate and cyclosporine oral DMARDs.
